name: Oatmeal / fibre for gut-skin axis

lead: Fibre-rich foods such as oatmeal are eaten to feed gut bacteria, with the hope of clearer skin through a proposed gut-skin axis. It is a common talking point in appearance communities.

The chain: gut bacteria ferment fibre into short-chain fatty acids (butyrate, propionate, acetate), which are linked to gut-barrier and immune functions, and the idea is that this calms inflammation that could show up in the skin. Fibre has documented effects, including lower cardiovascular risk associations and relief of constipation, and oat beta-glucan lowers LDL cholesterol. Skin outcomes have not been studied in the sources reviewed.

paras: People add oats, barley, beans, vegetables and other high-fibre foods to daily meals, most often with oatmeal as breakfast. The change is gradual, and users report digestion effects first.
Inulin can cause flatulence and digestive distress above about 15 g per day, and isolated fermentable fibres may cause bloating and gas. Raising fibre gradually is the usual way people avoid this.

angle.text: Users eat oats and other fibre to feed gut bacteria that make short-chain fatty acids, hoping for clearer skin through a proposed gut-skin axis. Fibre has documented gut and cholesterol effects; its effect on skin has not been studied.

lead: Eating oatmeal and other high-fibre foods is discussed in appearance circles as a way to support clearer, calmer skin from the inside. The reasoning follows the 'gut-skin axis': fermentable fibre feeds gut bacteria that produce short-chain fatty acids, which are described as having anti-inflammatory and gut-barrier roles that may be reflected in the skin.[1][2]

Dietary fibre is the portion of plant food not fully broken down by human digestive enzymes, including cellulose, resistant starch and pectins.[1] Oats and barley contain beta-glucan, a soluble viscous fermentable fibre that has been shown to lower LDL cholesterol with regular intake.[1] A 2016 review of oats notes that the link between oat beta-glucan and cardiovascular risk and glycaemia is established, while effects on intestinal microbiota and inflammation continue to be explored.[3]

A 2018 review in Frontiers in Microbiology by Salem and colleagues described the gut-skin axis as a proposed two-way link between intestinal microbes and skin, with short-chain fatty acids such as butyrate produced when gut bacteria ferment fibre.[2] The authors also noted that much of the supporting evidence comes from animal studies and small human trials, and that several mechanisms remain hypotheses.[2]

paras: Fermentable fibres feed bacteria in the large intestine, which produce short-chain fatty acids and gases; the main acids are butyrate, propionate and acetate. Wikipedia links them to steadier blood glucose, lower LDL, nourishment of colon cells and immune and gut-barrier functions.[1]

Salem and colleagues describe butyrate and related acids as promoting regulatory T cells and suppressing inflammation, and propose that they may also shape skin microbial communities and keratinocyte differentiation.[2] They argue that a low-fibre, high-fat Western diet reduces short-chain fatty acid production, and link a high-glycaemic diet to acne through insulin/IGF-1 and mTORC1 signalling.[2]

Oats have a long history as human food, originating in the Fertile Crescent, and contain macro-, micro- and phytonutrients that the 2016 review describes as giving them a high nutritional value.[3] A randomized trial published in the British Journal of Nutrition examined how oatmeal porridge affects microflora-associated characteristics in healthy subjects.[4]

Colloidal oatmeal, finely ground oats used in creams and baths, is a centuries-old topical treatment for rashes, itch and eczema, and laboratory work has examined its anti-inflammatory and antioxidant activity.[5] A randomized study of a 1% colloidal oat eczema cream compared it with a standard moisturizer on skin microbiome and barrier function in people with mild to moderate eczema.[6] These concern topical use, not oatmeal eaten for gut effects.

Inulin can cause flatulence and digestive distress in most people above about 15 g per day, isolated fermentable fibres may cause bloating, and finely ground insoluble fibre may cause constipation.[1]

No studies found on eating oatmeal or fibre for skin or acne outcomes. For general health, Wikipedia reports associations between high fibre intake and lower cardiovascular and type 2 diabetes risk and relief of constipation, described as preliminary.[1] Gut-skin axis research on diet, short-chain fatty acids and probiotics in acne, atopic dermatitis and psoriasis is reviewed by Salem and colleagues, who note that many human trials are small and some uncontrolled.[2]

timeline.event: A review in Advances in Food and Nutrition Research summarizes oats from origins to modern foods, noting ongoing study of microbiota and inflammation effects.[3]
Salem, Ramser, Isham and Ghannoum publish a review of the gut microbiome as a regulator of the gut-skin axis.[2]
